title: How Much to Save Monthly to Retire With $1 Million
description: The 'Compound Interest' roadmap from age 20 to 50.
content:
One million dollars is the psychological benchmark for wealth. While inflation has eroded its purchasing power, it remains a substantial nest egg that can generate ~$40,000/year in passive income forever. The path to $1M is purely mathematical: it is a function of when you start and how much you save. Starting early allows you to use 'other people's money' (market returns) to build the pile. Starting late requires you to use your own labor (high savings rate). This guide provides the exact monthly contributions needed to hit the seven-figure mark.

Key Takeaways

  • The 20-Year Gap: A 25-year-old needs to save ~$300/mo to hit $1M. A 45-year-old needs to save ~$1,700/mo. Waiting costs you exponential effort.
  • The 'Doubling' Period: At 7% returns, money doubles every 10 years. The first $100k takes the longest; the growth from $500k to $1M often happens in just 7-8 years.
  • Employer Match Acceleration: If your boss matches $200/mo, that counts toward your total. The 'money' doesn't all have to come from your paycheck.
  • Inflation Check: $1M in 30 years won't buy what $1M buys today. You should aim to increase your contribution by 3% annually to target '$1M of today's purchasing power'.

Why It Matters (US Context)

The S&P 500 historical average is ~10% (nominal). Adjusting for inflation, we typically use 7% for planning. This guide assumes a retirement age of 65 and a 7% annual return.

The Monthly Payment to Future You

To reach $1,000,000 at Age 65 (assuming 7% return, starting from $0).

Starting at Age 20 (45 Years)

Monthly Contribution: $260.

Insight: This is the cost of a cheap car lease. Anyone with a full-time job can technically afford to be a millionaire if they start day one.

Starting at Age 30 (35 Years)

Monthly Contribution: $550.

Insight: The cost doubled, but is still manageable (roughly maxing an IRA).

Starting at Age 40 (25 Years)

Monthly Contribution: $1,250.

Insight: You now need to max out an IRA and put $600 into a 401(k). Lifestyle sacrifices are required.

Starting at Age 50 (15 Years)

Monthly Contribution: $3,200.

Insight: This requires a high income and catch-up contributions ($30,500 limit). You are sprinting.

How to Hit the Number

  1. Automate the IRA: Set up a $583/mo transfer to a Roth IRA. This alone gets a 30-year-old to $1M tax-free.
  2. The 1% Escalator: You don't have to start at the max. Start at 3%. Increase your 401(k) contribution by 1% every January. You won't feel the change, but you'll hit the goal.
  3. Bank Windfalls: If you start late, you rely on 'Chunks'. Tax refunds, bonuses, and inheritance must go 100% to the portfolio. You don't have the luxury of spending windfalls.
  4. Asset Allocation: To hit 7% returns, you need stocks (Equities). If you leave the money in Cash/Bonds earning 3%, the monthly requirement doubles. You must take market risk.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is $1M enough to retire?

It provides ~$40,000/year passive income. Combined with Social Security ($25k-$35k), that is ~$70,000/year. For a paid-off homeowner, yes. For a renter in NYC, no.

What if I have $50k already?

That helps massively. $50k invested at 30 grows to $500k on its own by 65. You only need to save enough to bridge the other $500k.

Should I include inflation?

Using 7% return (instead of 10%) effectively adjusts for inflation. $1M in 'future dollars' will be a bigger number, but this math aims for $1M of purchasing power.
